title: Young stars sculpt gas with powerful outflows
caption: The star cluster NGC 346 and star-forming region N66, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
credit: NASA, ESA and A. Nota (ESA/STScI, STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: Ranked #22 on ESA/Hubble’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: A brilliant cluster of stars sits at the centre of this view, ringed by arched, ragged filaments with a distinct ridge. The dark edge of that ridge, seen in silhouette, is beaded with fine detail. This is NGC 346, the cluster at the heart of the star-forming region N66 in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.

The region is one of the most active and intricately structured places where stars are being born. Hot stars in the cluster give off a torrent of radiation that eats into the denser gas around them, carving the dust and gas into sculpted shapes.

Several small globules of dust sit along the ridge. Each one points back toward the central cluster, like a windsock caught in a strong wind. That alignment suggests they are being shaped by the radiation streaming outward from the young stars at the centre.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys took this view through visible, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters. The colour assigned to each filter isn't published.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light that the eye cannot see, and the long exposures reveal fine dusty detail no eye could pick out at this distance.

explore: The region lies about 210,000 light-years away, far beyond our own galaxy, in the direction of the constellation Tucana. Hubble's view shows how the radiation from a young cluster can reshape the cloud in which its stars were born.
alt: A bright star cluster at the centre surrounded by arched, ragged filaments of gas and a dark, beaded ridge of dust seen in silhouette.
